questions.stem: Which is a typical challenge of the growth stage of the business life cycle?
options: keeping up with rising demand without letting quality or service slip
testing whether anyone wants the product before it is launched
deciding whether to close a business whose sales are falling
finding a very first customer for a product that has never been sold before
questions.explanation: In the growth stage, sales rise quickly, stretching staff, systems, cash and quality control. Testing demand and finding first customers belong to the seed and start-up stages.

questions.stem: A fast-growing Gold Coast skincare brand takes on more orders than its cash and staff can support, and struggles to pay suppliers. This problem is best described as:
options: market saturation, because the brand has no remaining customers left to win
a decline in brand awareness among its target market
a seed-stage challenge of raising finance for an unproven idea
overtrading, expanding faster than the business's resources allow
questions.explanation: Overtrading occurs when growth outruns the cash and capacity needed to fund it, so even a successful business can run short of cash. The brand clearly has demand, so saturation and falling awareness do not fit.

questions.stem: Which marketing objective is most relevant when a business wants more people to recognise and remember its brand?
options: market share
sales revenue
cost reduction
brand awareness
questions.explanation: Brand awareness measures how familiar the target market is with the brand. Market share compares the business's sales with the total market, and cost reduction is not a marketing objective.

questions.stem: A Brisbane coffee roaster's sales were $1.8 million in a local market worth $12 million. What is its market share?
questions.explanation: Market share = 1.8 ÷ 12 × 100 = 15%. Dividing the market by the business's sales gives 6.7, which is not a percentage share.

questions.stem: A business's sales rose by 10%, but its market share fell from 20% to 18%. What does this show?
options: the business's sales must have fallen, because market share fell
the business is now the market leader, because its own sales increased by 10%
the total market shrank, so every business lost sales
the total market grew faster than the business, so competitors gained ground
questions.explanation: If sales rise while share falls, the whole market must have grown faster than the business's sales, meaning rivals grew more. Sales objectives and market share objectives can move in different directions.

questions.stem: The total product concept includes:
options: the business's legal structure and its method of finance
the core benefit, the tangible product and intangible extras such as warranties and service
only the physical features of the product that a customer can see, touch and compare
only the price that the customer pays at the point of sale
questions.explanation: Customers buy a bundle: the core benefit they want, the tangible product with its features, brand and packaging, and intangible aspects such as after-sales service, warranty and delivery.

questions.stem: A Townsville bike shop offers free servicing for a year with every new bike. Which aspect of the total product concept is this?
options: the core benefit that the customer is really buying when choosing a bike
a tangible feature of the bike's design
a psychological pricing strategy
an intangible aspect that adds value beyond the bike itself
questions.explanation: Free servicing is an intangible part of the offer that augments the physical bike and can differentiate it from rivals. The core benefit is the transport or recreation the bike provides.

questions.stem: Why is consistent branding especially important during the growth stage?
options: consistent branding removes the need for any promotion when the business enters new markets
brands only matter once a business reaches the decline stage
consistent branding guarantees the lowest prices in the market
a recognisable brand helps build a loyal customer base and market presence as the business expands
questions.explanation: Branding, a customer base and market presence reinforce each other: a consistent, recognisable brand makes the business easier to remember and trust as it enters new markets, which builds loyal customers and presence. Promotion is still needed.

questions.stem: As its products become popular, a growing snack brand registers its name and logo as trade marks. What is the main benefit?
options: the brand and its products become exempt from the Australian Consumer Law and the ACCC
the business no longer needs to register a business name
the products are automatically protected by a patent
competitors cannot legally use a similar name or logo to trade on its reputation
questions.explanation: A registered trade mark gives exclusive rights to use the brand for the registered goods, protecting the reputation built during growth. It does not exempt the business from consumer law or patent its products.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an emerging promotional platform rather than a traditional one?
options: a livestream on a social platform where viewers can buy products as they are shown
a full-page advertisement in a regional daily newspaper
a 30-second television commercial shown during the evening news on a commercial network
a large billboard beside a major highway
questions.explanation: Livestream shopping, augmented reality try-ons and influencer partnerships are emerging platforms. Newspapers, television and billboards are traditional media.

questions.stem: A growing fitness app pays several well-known fitness creators to show the app in their videos. Which promotional strategy is this?
options: a cost-plus pricing strategy
a sales promotion in a physical store
influencer marketing on digital platforms
traditional print advertising
questions.explanation: Paying creators with large followings to feature a product is influencer marketing. Under the ACL and advertising codes, such paid content must be clearly disclosed as advertising.

questions.stem: A Mackay hardware store wants to reach older local tradespeople and also younger first-home buyers. Which promotional mix is most suitable?
options: only social media, because every age group uses it in exactly the same way
only national television, because the widest possible reach is always the best choice
no promotion, because existing customers will tell everyone about the store
local radio and newspaper for older trades, plus targeted social media for young buyers
questions.explanation: Matching media to each segment's habits is more effective than relying on a single channel. National television would waste money on people outside the store's area.

questions.stem: Competitive pricing means:
options: ending prices in 95 or 99 cents to make them seem lower to shoppers
setting prices at, or close to, the prices charged by rivals
adding a fixed percentage to the cost of each product
starting with a high price and lowering it over time
questions.explanation: Competitive pricing uses rivals' prices as the guide, common where products are similar. Adding a percentage to cost is cost plus, starting high is cream-skimming, and prices ending in 99 are psychological.

questions.stem: A business uses cost-plus pricing with a 25% mark-up on cost. If a product costs $40, what is its selling price?
questions.explanation: Selling price = 40 + (25% × 40) = $50. Treating 25% as a margin on the selling price gives 40 ÷ 0.75 = $53.33, which is a different calculation.

questions.stem: A clothing store prices a jacket at $79.95 instead of $80. Which pricing strategy is this?
options: psychological pricing
cost-plus pricing
cream-skimming
competitive pricing
questions.explanation: Psychological pricing uses prices just below a round number so they seem noticeably cheaper. The five-cent difference has nothing to do with costs or rivals' prices.

questions.stem: A new gaming headset with unique features is launched at a high price for keen early buyers, and the price is reduced after a year. Which strategy is this, and when does it suit?
options: cost-plus pricing; it suits products where demand is unknown and costs are uncertain
cream-skimming; it suits innovative products with few competitors and buyers willing to pay more
penetration pricing; it suits products entering a crowded market with many rivals
competitive pricing; it suits products identical to those of many rivals
questions.explanation: Cream-skimming, or price skimming, charges a high initial price to recover development costs from early adopters, then lowers it to reach more buyers. It works when the product is new and distinctive.

questions.stem: In operations, capacity refers to:
options: the number of different customers who have bought from the business
the amount of finance the business can borrow
the share of the market held by the business
the maximum output a business can produce in a given period
questions.explanation: Capacity is the most a facility, team or process can produce in a set time, such as meals per night or units per week. It limits how fast a growing business can meet demand.

questions.stem: A bakery can produce 2,400 loaves a week but currently makes 1,800. What is its capacity utilisation?
questions.explanation: Capacity utilisation = 1,800 ÷ 2,400 × 100 = 75%. The 25% figure is the unused capacity, and dividing the other way gives 133%.

questions.stem: During the growth stage, a café introduces a staff rostering system that puts more staff on during the busy breakfast period. Which operational practice is this?
options: inventory management
market research
scheduling
facilities design
questions.explanation: Scheduling arranges people, equipment and tasks over time to meet demand efficiently. Facilities design concerns the premises and layout, and inventory management concerns stock.

questions.stem: A growing furniture maker's orders now exceed its workshop's capacity, and it holds very little timber in stock. What is the most likely result, and the best response?
options: lower costs and higher sales; reduce capacity even further to save on wages and rent
no effect on customers; keep operations unchanged until demand falls
excess inventory; cut timber orders and stop accepting new customers
delays and lost orders; increase capacity and hold enough timber to support production
questions.explanation: Inventories, production and capacity are linked: without enough materials or capacity, production cannot meet orders, so customers wait or go elsewhere. Expanding capacity, for example through extra shifts or equipment, and holding sufficient stock addresses the problem.

questions.stem: Why is customer service an important operational practice for a business in the growth stage?
options: good service guarantees that the business's costs will fall
good service turns new customers into repeat customers who recommend the business
customer service only really matters once a business has stopped growing altogether
customer service replaces the need for quality products
questions.explanation: As a business attracts new customers, service quality shapes whether they return and spread positive word of mouth. Service works alongside, not instead of, good products.

questions.stem: A SWOT analysis of a growing online retailer's operations lists 'fast, reliable warehouse' as a strength and 'courier price rises' as a threat. Which conclusion is most valid?
options: the business should keep its speed advantage while seeking cheaper or shared delivery options
the business should close its warehouse, as courier prices are an internal weakness
the warehouse is an opportunity and the courier prices are a strength
the two factors are unrelated, so neither has any implication for operations
questions.explanation: Interpreting the relationship shows a strength in fulfilment that rising external delivery costs could erode, so the business should protect its advantage while managing the threat. Courier prices are external, so they are a threat, not a weakness.

questions.stem: A unique selling proposition (USP) is:
options: the list of all products a business sells, arranged by price
the feature or benefit that makes a product different from and better than competitors' in customers' eyes
the lowest price that a business can charge for a product without making a loss on each sale it makes
the total value of a business's sales in its first year of trading
questions.explanation: A USP is the distinctive reason customers should choose one business's offering over its rivals'. It can be based on quality, service, convenience, innovation or price, but it must be unique and valued.

questions.stem: A USP analysis of three Toowoomba pizza shops shows: Shop A has the lowest prices; Shop B uses wood-fired ovens and local produce; Shop C offers the fastest delivery. A new entrant plans average prices, average quality and average delivery. What is the most valid conclusion?
options: it will win the most customers, because being average on every feature appeals to everyone
it has three USPs, because it matches all three competitors at once
it does not need a USP, because pizza is a product everyone buys
it has no clear USP, so it will struggle to attract customers from the established shops
questions.explanation: Each competitor owns a distinct position, so a business that is average on all three gives customers no reason to switch. The analysis suggests finding an unfilled point of difference.

questions.stem: How is market research related to sales forecasting?
options: sales forecasting replaces the need for any market research
research data on demand, trends and competitors is used to estimate future sales
sales forecasts are made first and then used to invent market research findings
market research and sales forecasting are unrelated activities
questions.explanation: Forecasts rely on information from past sales, surveys, industry data and competitor analysis. Accurate forecasts then guide production, inventory and staffing decisions.

questions.stem: Market research shows that a growing Cairns juice bar's customers now value low-sugar options and reusable cups. How should this most affect its marketing mix?
options: add low-sugar drinks, offer a reusable-cup discount and promote both to existing customers
keep the menu unchanged, as consumer behaviour does not affect the marketing mix
raise all prices, because research always shows customers will pay more
stop all promotion, because research shows customers already know the brand
questions.explanation: Market research reveals consumer behaviour, and the marketing mix of product, price, place and promotion should respond to it. Changes in behaviour should lead to changes in the mix.

questions.stem: A growing business advertises 'Australia's cheapest broadband' without any evidence. Which body would most likely take action, and why?
options: the Australian Taxation Office, because the claim affects the GST payable
Ad Standards, because it can fine businesses for breaches of the Competition and Consumer Act
IP Australia, because the claim breaches the business's trade mark
the ACCC, because the claim may be misleading or deceptive under the Australian Consumer Law
questions.explanation: The ACCC enforces the Australian Consumer Law, which prohibits misleading or deceptive conduct and false claims. Ad Standards handles complaints about advertising content under industry codes but does not enforce the Competition and Consumer Act.

questions.stem: What is the role of Ad Standards in Australian advertising?
options: it sets the maximum prices that businesses may charge for products they advertise nationally
it approves every advertisement before it can be published
it manages a complaints system for advertising content under industry codes of practice
it registers trade marks and business names for advertisers
questions.explanation: Ad Standards administers the self-regulatory complaints process, with a community panel deciding whether ads breach industry codes on matters such as decency and health and safety. Ads are not pre-approved by it, and trade marks are registered by IP Australia.

questions.stem: Before a national launch, a growing supplement brand wants to claim its product 'boosts immunity'. What should it do to comply with the ACCC's expectations and advertising standards?
options: make the claim in small print only, so it is not technically part of the advertisement
avoid the issue by making the claim only on social media, where consumer law does not apply
make the claim, because advertising standards apply only to television commercials
hold reliable evidence for the claim and make sure the advertising is accurate and not misleading
questions.explanation: Claims must be truthful and able to be substantiated, whatever the medium; consumer law and advertising codes apply to digital and social media too. Fine print cannot correct a misleading overall impression.

questions.stem: A growing Sunshine Coast brewery must choose between doubling its brewing capacity or contracting another brewery to produce half its beer. Using the business criteria, which point favours contracting?
options: it meets rising demand quickly without a large investment, though quality control may be harder
it guarantees higher quality, because outside brewers always follow the brand's recipes exactly
it removes all costs of production, so the business's profit must rise
it is always more competitive, because customers prefer beer made by other brewers
questions.explanation: Contracting can be efficient and effective in the short term, avoiding capital outlay while meeting demand, but it reduces control over quality and consistency, which may affect stakeholder satisfaction. It still involves paying the contractor.
